title: QUIC server-side resumption ticket issuance architecture
purpose: Define the first managed server-side resumption-ticket issuance seam without widening the public resumption promise or claiming PSK acceptance.
design_summary: Server ticket issuance is opt-in through internal managed-server configuration so the default server path and public API promise remain unchanged. The managed TLS key schedule emits a TLS 1.3 NewSessionTicket after the server verifies the peer Finished and derives 1-RTT packet-protection material. Post-handshake ticket bytes use the existing TLS CRYPTO publication model at the 1-RTT encryption level, with the runtime formatting those bytes into a QUIC CRYPTO frame before protecting an application-data packet. The ticket body is intentionally opaque to the public surface and carries no early_data extension, so the slice does not imply 0-RTT acceptance, server anti-replay, or replayable early-data delivery. Server-side PSK identity caching, binder validation, ServerHello pre_shared_key selection, and resumed PSK-DHE key-schedule derivation remain separate follow-on work.
edge_cases_and_constraints: Server ticket issuance remains internal and opt-in.
Default managed server behavior remains ticket-free.
The ticket omits early_data and carries no 0-RTT acceptance promise.
The slice does not add server-side PSK cache sharing, binder validation, resumed ServerHello selection, PSK-DHE derivation, public API widening, or HTTP/3 interop.
alternatives_considered: Expose a public resumption-ticket option. Rejected because the support promise is still blocked on PSK acceptance and resumed handshake derivation.

Treat client-side ticket capture as sufficient for resumption interop. Rejected because quic-interop-runner needs the managed server to issue a ticket before later resumed-handshake work can be exercised.
Emit early_data-capable tickets in this slice. Rejected because server anti-replay and 0-RTT admission are not implemented.
risks: If the internal opt-in switch leaks into the public API, callers could infer resumption support before resumed PSK acceptance exists.
If ticket emission is not bound to peer Finished verification and 1-RTT key availability, post-handshake TLS bytes can be published at the wrong cryptographic boundary.
If follow-on PSK cache and binder validation work treats this opaque ticket as sufficient, resumed connection acceptance could be under-specified.
